scenes.heading: Expanding and special products
scenes.say: Is x plus five, all squared, the same as x squared plus twenty-five? Lots of students think so, but it isn't. In this video you will learn to expand brackets and spot the special patterns that make it quick.
scenes.caption: Is (x + 5)² the same as x² + 25? Lots of students think so, but it isn't. In this video you will learn to expand brackets and spot the special patterns that make it quick.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Two pairs of friends meet: everyone shakes everyone's hand, 4 handshakes
scenes.science: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd
scenes.breaks: Handshakes never merge, but like terms do combine, so you often end with 3 terms.
scenes.say: Picture two pairs of friends meeting. Each person shakes hands with each person in the other pair, so there are four handshakes. Expanding two brackets is the same: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second. Then you collect any like terms.

scenes.heading: Perfect squares
scenes.say: A bracket times itself is a perfect square. Square the first term, double the product, and square the last term. The middle sign matches the sign in the bracket.
scenes.caption: A bracket times itself is a perfect square. Square the first term, double the product, and square the last term. The middle sign matches the sign in the bracket.

scenes.heading: Where 2ab comes from
scenes.say: First a square with side a plus b. Then we split it: a big square, a squared, a small square, b squared, and two rectangles, each a times b. Two rectangles means the middle term is two a b. That's why x plus five squared has a ten x in it.
scenes.caption: First a square with side a + b. Split it: a², b², and two rectangles, each ab. Two rectangles means the middle term is 2ab. That's why (x + 5)² has a 10x in it.

scenes.heading: Difference of two squares
scenes.say: When two brackets match except for the sign, the middle terms cancel. You're left with a squared minus b squared, the difference of two squares. For example, three x plus four, times three x minus four, is nine x squared minus sixteen.
scenes.caption: When two brackets match except for the sign, the middle terms cancel: a² − b². For example, (3x + 4)(3x − 4) = 9x² − 16.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Expand (3x − 5)².
scenes.say: Expand three x minus five, all squared. Here a is three x and b is five. a squared is nine x squared. Two a b is two times three x times five, thirty x. b squared is twenty-five. So the answer is nine x squared minus thirty x plus twenty-five.
scenes.caption: Expand (3x − 5)². a = 3x and b = 5. a² = 9x², 2ab = 30x, b² = 25. Answer: 9x² − 30x + 25.

scenes.heading: Subtracting a product
scenes.question: Expand and simplify (x + 3)² − (x − 2)(x + 5).
scenes.say: Expand each part first. x plus three squared is x squared plus six x plus nine. The product is x squared plus three x minus ten. Keep it in brackets, then subtract every term, so minus ten becomes plus ten. That leaves three x plus nineteen.
scenes.caption: Expand each part first: x² + 6x + 9 and x² + 3x − 10. Keep the product in brackets, then subtract every term, so −10 becomes +10. Answer: 3x + 19.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Multiply every term by every term. Perfect squares have a middle term of two a b. The difference of two squares has no middle term. When you subtract a product, change every sign. And check by substituting x equals one. Now try the practice questions!
